Eu não gostei do filme Conclave porque ele passa uma visão muito mais humana e política da Igreja do que espiritual. Em vários momentos, parece que tudo gira em torno de interesses, estratégias e disputas de poder, deixando de lado aquilo que, para mim, é essencial: a ação de Deus e a condução do Espírito Santo. Além disso, senti que o filme pode confundir quem assiste, principalmente quem não conhece bem a fé católica, dando a impressão de que o conclave é apenas um jogo de influência entre cardeais. Isso me incomodou, porque acaba enfraquecendo a verdadeira dimensão sagrada e espiritual desse momento tão importante para a Igreja. Outro ponto é que algumas atitudes e comportamentos mostrados parecem exagerados ou até distorcidos, o que me fez questionar se aquilo realmente representa a realidade ou se foi criado apenas para gerar drama. Para mim, isso tirou um pouco da credibilidade da história. No geral, eu esperava algo que fortalecesse mais a fé ou mostrasse melhor a beleza e a profundidade da Igreja, mas acabei encontrando uma narrativa mais voltada para conflitos humanos. Por isso, não foi um filme que me agradou.

I actually liked the religious themes because religion is one of my favorite themes to see explored in movies. However, I felt like Conclave took those ideas in a direction that didn’t work for me. The movie builds itself up like it is going to decide the future and fate of the Church, but I couldn’t fully take some of those moments seriously because they felt too exaggerated, which ended up making the story feel dull. Spoilers: The last few minutes were the biggest problem for me. The final reveal felt completely unnecessary and like it was inserted just to shock the audience. Instead of strengthening the themes that were already being explored, it changed the entire meaning of the story and made everything that came before feel different. It was a huge “what was the point of this?” moment for me, and it ultimately made the movie not work.

После смерти Папы Римского кардиналы собираются для выбора нового главы католической церкви. Процесс превращается в настоящую борьбу, ведь у каждого кандидата оказывается свой скелет в шкафу. Зрителя погружают в атмосферу мрачных коридоров Ватикана. Звукорежиссёр позволяет услышать шаги, шёпот и даже дыхание героев, что одновременно создаёт напряжение и интимную обстановку для обсуждения вопросов веры. Сохранение традиции или реформа религиозных институтов? Глава церкви - менеджер или пастырь? Может ли он сомневаться? Какие человеческие слабости нельзя в нём принять? Все эти вопросы практически не поднимаются в "Конклаве". Триллер здесь тоже сложно найти. Главный герой узнает тайну одного из кандидатов, делает её публичной, баланс сил на голосовании меняется - и так несколько раз. Тогда зачем это всё нужно? Ответ разочаровывающе банален: фильм является реакцией на выборы в странах Запада. Да, это очередное обсуждение "правых популистов", "левых либералов" и прочих словосочетаний, не вызывающих уже ничего, кроме скуки. Хорошо, фильм хочет говорить про политику, а не про религию. Будет ли здесь показан интересный конфликт идей? Нет. В самом начале зрителю чётко говорят: "Вот правые, они очень плохие. Вот левые, они хорошие, но им чего-то не хватает для победы". Ни аргументов, ни дискуссии здесь не будет. То есть, чтобы сопереживать местной драме, нужно заранее находиться в определённой части политического спектра. Финал фильма, когда зритель узнает, кто и в какой обстановке победил Главного Буржуина, может вызвать только нервный смешок.

Still pissed off at the ending. The first 115 minutes are incredible and tackle issues of faith, ideology, and how politics factor into a decision that should be divinely inspired. The different ways that each favorite for the papacy balances their personal and spiritual ambitions is presented in a thrilling way. The only way to make the ending make any sense within the greater extent of the film is to assume that the true intention all along was an exploration of the role of gender/sex in the church and the arbitrary requirement for priests, etc. to be male. However, if that is the case, the previous length of the movie does a really bad job of setting that up, as in the scenes in which gender comes up it is overshadowed by other events that drive the obvious plot forward. This could have been one of my favorite movies, but unfortunately they flew close to the sun and tried to make one "powerful" statement too many.

Additionally, over 100 cardinals attended the conclave from all around the globe, meaning they speak different languages. The director took an artistic approach by deliberately omitting subtitles. I personally found it confusing and had to guess what characters were saying based on body language when there easily could have been on-screen text. I also don't understand how the boss nun was nominated for Best Supporting Actress when she was barely in the film. Conclave just wasn't for me. I know it got nominated for a ton of awards but I just couldn’t get into it like I wanted to. The awards for this movie should be for acting and how the movie visually looked, not for the storyline. In terms of storyline, I felt that The DaVinci Code did a much better job portraying secrets and cover-ups within the Church and more specifically conclave.

Just so utterly shallow. This movie seems to want you to question certain things about the Church, its structure, and Catholicism as a whole, but it spends most of its time building on the political thriller aspect instead. Yes, we all understand that politics is embedded in nearly every facet of life whether we want it to be or not. But the movie exaggerates this to an almost goofy degree while being incredibly intentional and not particularly clever about it. Tedesco is the most obvious example. He is essentially the villain trope meant to represent the “bad traditions” of the Church. He unironically has some good points, but his character is so exaggerated that he loses any sense of realism. I wish the movie actually grappled with some of what he was saying rather than making him so obviously the person we are supposed to reject. I really did like the aspect of the movie that dealt with human imperfection. There are some great lines of dialogue here, particularly, “We’re mortal men. We serve an ideal. We cannot always be ideal.” I think the movie is at its strongest when it leans into this idea because it naturally complements the political thriller at its core. These are supposed to be men serving something greater than themselves, yet they remain flawed, ambitious, uncertain human beings. There is something genuinely interesting there. Yet the ending completely loses the plot for me. The first major event already feels quite random and unrealistic, but then the movie completely loses me with a final plot twist that ultimately serves no real purpose. It feels like the writers wanted to introduce an extremely provocative question but were too scared to actually take it to its logical extreme, instead landing on something that feels utterly useless and impractical. I agree that the circumstances are peculiar and could raise an interesting question for the Church, but throwing this in at the last possible second just feels ridiculous. I also feel the need to bring up the completely undeveloped plot line/message of the matter of women’s role in the church. One scene is just so blatantly to the point and seemingly out of nowhere. I feel like there was an attempt to flesh out something here but in my opinion it just falls completely flat. There is some genuinely good dialogue throughout. Lawrence’s sermon about certainty and doubt, for example, is probably one of the strongest parts of the movie. But I think the movie’s obvious guiding hand in its message, particularly its support for religious diversification and liberalism within the Church, ultimately gets in its own way. I wish both sides of that spectrum had actually been challenged. Instead, the movie seems to know from the beginning which side is correct and constructs its characters accordingly. Some great performances, no doubt, but I cannot say much else good about this one. I think this is probably a very good movie if you do not think too much about any real-life Church or religious context. It’s suspenseful, well shot, and ultimately hopeful. Unfortunately, I just cannot get past that disconnect. What could have been a genuinely interesting examination of faith, doubt, tradition, reform, and the imperfections of the people who serve the Church instead becomes an utter simplification and an almost black-and-white portrayal of the issues it wants to explore.

Conclave feels like a story about the difference between faith and certainty. It takes place inside one of the most powerful religious institutions in the world, but the film is less interested in religion itself than in what happens when human beings convince themselves they understand something greater than them. What makes the film resonate is how every cardinal carries his own idea of truth. They speak about God, tradition, and morality, but underneath those beliefs are ambition, fear, ego, and insecurity. The conclave becomes a reminder that even the most sacred institutions are still operated by imperfect people. Lawrence is what gives the story its emotional weight. His crisis of faith isn't portrayed as weakness. If anything, his doubt makes him one of the few people capable of genuine reflection. The film quietly suggests that certainty can be more dangerous than disbelief because certainty leaves no room for humility. What lingers is the idea that faith might require doubt. To believe while acknowledging you could be wrong is completely different from using belief as proof of your own righteousness. The characters most convinced of their moral purity often seem the least capable of questioning themselves. The final revelation reinforces everything the film has been asking. Humanity constantly tries to create categories, rules, and structures to make existence easier to understand. But life has never been obligated to fit neatly inside them. Conclave stays with me because it suggests that maybe the opposite of faith isn't doubt. Maybe it's certainty. The moment you believe you have all the answers is often the moment you stop searching for truth.

Conclave is beautiful in every way; a mystery of many locked boxes and a ritual of politics & grief that flows between ecclesiastical drama, internal struggle and the quiet mundane. The framing and design of the architecture show a hostile opulence across time, that which secludes and outlives all, just as each marble hotel room bears witness to just a few nights of its occupant's life. An ancient ritual persists with electronic locks and x-ray security, espresso machines and hotel toiletries. Just as much attention is given to the bus ride and meals times as rounds of voting - each process is just as important in how it determines who will be the spiritual leader of m/billions. Through the mundanities, the conclave is demystified; however, we are still kept at arms reach, barred not only from participation, but knowledge of every other iteration, left to wonder about the thousands of cardinals (and sisters) of the Curia throughout history, the decisions made and the influence they have had on world events. The very brief extract of choral music we get is just divine, it's no wonder pre-modern folks heard the beauty of the heavens in it as it echoed through those high ceilings. The homily that follows is such a beautiful (hopeful) distillation of faith in the modern age, faith as something that breathes and changes, something human that should be in conversation with doubt and interpretation, a united church of mutual respect and integration and openness. In order to believe, one must accept that they cannot fully understand. Interspersed with grand affairs of scandal, there's a real tenderness to the scenes in between: the stillness of a dead man's room, left lived-in and undisturbed; letting yourself feel the grief of a dear friend lost when you has to keep it together for so long; asking someone to quietly pray with you while you're whole world is falling down. Bit of a tacked-on twist ending, but that's the book's fault, and apparently the author has been locked into a twisty Shyamalan brand that harms his ability to tell a good story. Nevertheless, through this and his other interactions with Cardinal Benitez, Cardinal Lawrence, a Church 'Liberal', is able to truly heed his own words. I know it would be hard to track, but I really feel like you shouldn't be able to vote for yourself in the conclave...

Conclave delves within the procedure of how the highest order of the church elects a new holy leader following previous' passing or departure. In this movie, it shows that the process can be complicated in addition to its secrecy. It carries a thought-provoking notion presenting that a holy institute is still just an institution. In this case, its foundation is built with body and blood. "Not in God. What he had lost faith in was the Church." Is the movie pro-religion? Nope. Is it anti-Christian? Not really. Is it human? Yes, most definitely! Furthermore, it presents that despite being put in a position of a holy order, those people who upholds a spiritual doctrine with the highest regards can still fall into a episodes of spiritual crisis, impostor syndrome, or growing suspision among comrades. In a worst case scenario, a person put within this heavy-burden position can be corrupted into a radical political crusade based on unjust ambitious or greed, discrimination against the other faiths, or a deep dive into unfolding further scandals. To top it all off, with that distinct yet powerful conclusion that would make you question "what would be the major political and religious discourse if this actually happened or how would this challenge the church's tradition as a whole?" It is really raw and relevant stuff that could really happen or have already happened within the real world. Overall, the movie is trying to tell that the notion of faith is now a personal spiritual battle in our morally grey world: For some of those who certainly believe can even lead us back to a dark age.
